greek.title: The Pythagorean Invention of Cosmic Order
greek.body:
Pythagoras of Samos first called the universe κόσμος in the sixth century BCE, a word that meant both 'order' and 'ornament.' Before him, Greeks spoke of sky and earth as separate realms. His radical insight joined them: the heavens moved in mathematical harmony, the same ratios that pleased the ear on a lyre. The spheres sang.

This vision transformed Greek thought. Where Homer's world churned with divine caprice, Pythagoras saw pattern. The word itself captures this double meaning—the cosmos is ordered and therefore beautiful, beautiful because ordered. His followers wore white, abstained from beans, and studied geometry as a spiritual practice. They believed numbers were not mere tools but the substance of reality itself.

The term passed to Plato, then to the Stoics, who imagined the universe as a single breathing animal, rational and self-ordering. We inherit their word, emptied now of its original wonder.
